state.misconception_label: Does not know the properties of a rectangle

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The angles highlighted on this rectangle with different length sides can never be... ![A rectangle with the diagonals drawn in. The angle on the right hand side at the centre is highlighted in red and the angle at the bottom at the centre is highlighted in yellow.](). I got acute because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a rectangular piece of paper. If you fold it in half along the longest side, what do you notice about the angles where the fold is? This can help us understand why the angles highlighted on a rectangle with different length sides can never be equal.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see what you mean... so when I fold the paper, the angles at the fold aren't the same as the corners of the rectangle? But I'm still confused about the highlighted angles in the middle where the diagonals cross - why can't those be acute if the rectangle has different length sides?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a rectangular swimming pool. When you dive in from one side, you hit the bottom at an angle. But when you dive in from the opposite side, you hit the bottom at a different angle. This can help us understand why the angles at the center where the diagonals cross in a rectangle with different side lengths can never be acute.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, I think I'm starting to get it... so the diagonals in a rectangle always cross in the middle and make angles that are never really small or acute? But I'm still not totally sure why the different side lengths matter - like, does that mean the angles at the center have to be bigger than acute, like obtuse or right angles?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses confusing, inaccurate analogies (folding paper, swimming pool) that fail to address the student's specific misconception about angles formed by diagonals, and the student remains confused throughout, showing no improvement in understanding why the highlighted angles cannot be acute.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use real-world analogies (folding paper, swimming pool), these analogies are poorly connected to the mathematical concepts and fail to meaningfully ground the geometric relationships in concrete experience that would aid understanding.
